blocks.text: After drinking three litres of water, your urine may be as dilute as 50 mOsm/kg and plentiful; after a night without drinking it may be about 1000 mOsm/kg and scanty. Plasma is about 290 mOsm/kg throughout. The same kidneys can therefore make urine far more dilute or far more concentrated than blood, and the secret lies in what each segment of the nephron does to the filtrate.

blocks.markdown: The glomerulus filters about 180 L of fluid a day, yet only about 1.5 L leaves as urine. The tubule therefore **reabsorbs** (moves from lumen to blood) most of the water and solutes, and **secretes** (moves from blood to lumen) some others such as hydrogen ions, potassium and many drugs. Reabsorption of sodium by the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase powers most of this, and water follows by osmosis wherever the epithelium is water-permeable.

rows: About 65 per cent of filtered Na+ and water; essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids; most bicarbonate and phosphate; secretion of organic acids and bases and many drugs
Na+/glucose cotransporter SGLT2 (and SGLT1), Na+/H+ exchanger NHE3, Na+/K+ ATPase
High: fluid reabsorbed isosmotically (osmolality stays near 290 mOsm/kg)

High (water leaves into the hypertonic medulla)

blocks.title: Where does the filtered water go?
blocks.prompt: A person has a GFR of 180 L/day and produces 1.5 L of urine. If the proximal tubule reabsorbs 65 per cent of filtered water and the loop of Henle about 15 per cent, calculate the volume reabsorbed in each segment, and the amount reabsorbed by the distal tubule and collecting duct combined.

steps.text: Proximal tubule: 65 per cent of 180 L.
Loop of Henle: 15 per cent of 180 L (mainly the descending limb).
Remaining after both: 180 - 117 - 27 = 36 L. The final urine is 1.5 L, so the distal tubule and collecting duct reabsorb 36 - 1.5 = 34.5 L.

blocks.answer: The proximal tubule reabsorbs 117 L, the loop 27 L and the distal nephron 34.5 L, so about 99.2 per cent of the filtered water is reabsorbed. The distal tubule and collecting duct contribute about 19 per cent here, and it is this late portion that antidiuretic hormone adjusts according to need.

blocks.title: Glucose and the transport maximum
blocks.text: Filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed completely in the proximal tubule by sodium-glucose cotransporters. These carriers have a limited capacity (the transport maximum). When plasma glucose rises above the renal threshold (roughly 10 mmol/L, varying between people), the filtered load exceeds the carrier capacity and glucose appears in the urine (glycosuria). The unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule by osmosis, causing an osmotic diuresis with excess urine volume and thirst.

blocks.markdown: **The countercurrent mechanism.** To produce urine more concentrated than plasma, the kidney builds a gradient of osmolality in the medullary interstitium that increases from about 300 mOsm/kg at the corticomedullary border to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papillary tip. The loop of Henle, running down into and back up from the medulla, acts as a **countercurrent multiplier**. The key is the **single effect**: the thick ascending limb actively pumps NaCl out of the tubule (via NKCC2) but is impermeable to water, so it dilutes the tubular fluid and makes the interstitium hypertonic. The adjacent descending limb is water-permeable, so water leaves it until the fluid inside equilibrates with the hypertonic interstitium, concentrating the fluid as it descends. Because fluid flows in opposite directions in the two limbs, a small difference at each level is multiplied along the length of the loop.

blocks.title: Countercurrent multiplication and exchange
blocks.text: Countercurrent multiplication is the process by which opposed flows in the limbs of the loop of Henle, together with active NaCl transport in the thick ascending limb, build a large osmotic gradient along the medulla. Countercurrent exchange is the passive process in the vasa recta (the capillaries that accompany the loops) that removes water and solute without dissipating the gradient.

items: Thick ascending limb transports NaCl out of the lumen into the interstitium without water, so the interstitium becomes hypertonic and the fluid in the limb becomes dilute.
Water leaves the descending limb by osmosis, so the descending fluid becomes more concentrated as it descends towards the tip of the loop.

New isosmotic fluid continually enters from the proximal tubule, pushing concentrated fluid around the bend, so the gradient is multiplied from about 200 mOsm/kg at each horizontal level to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the tip.
Urea, recycled from the medullary collecting duct (where urea transporters are increased by ADH) into the interstitium, contributes about half of the medullary osmolality.
The vasa recta run in a hairpin; blood entering gains solute and loses water, and blood leaving does the reverse, so the gradient is preserved rather than washed out.

blocks.caption: The minimum urine volume (obligatory water loss) is set by the solute that must be excreted and the maximum urine osmolality the kidney can produce.

blocks.title: Why concentrating ability matters
blocks.prompt: A person must excrete 600 mOsm of solute a day. Calculate the daily urine volume if the urine osmolality is (a) 1200 mOsm/kg (taken as 1200 mOsm/L) and (b) 50 mOsm/L.

steps.text: Volume equals solute load divided by urine osmolality.
The range from 0.5 to 12 L/day shows how the countercurrent mechanism and ADH allow water to be conserved or excreted according to need.

blocks.answer: With maximal concentration the person needs to lose only 0.5 L/day of water to excrete the solute; with dilute urine 12 L/day would be passed.

blocks.markdown: **Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** is synthesised in the hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) and released from the posterior pituitary when osmoreceptors detect a rise in plasma osmolality (or when blood volume falls substantially). In the collecting duct, ADH binds **V2 receptors** on the basolateral membrane of principal cells; this activates a G-protein and adenylyl cyclase to raise cyclic AMP, and protein kinase A promotes the insertion of **aquaporin-2 (AQP2)** water channels into the luminal membrane. Water then moves out of the lumen through AQP2 and exits the cell through AQP3 and AQP4 in the basolateral membrane, down the osmotic gradient into the hypertonic medulla. With ADH the collecting duct becomes water-permeable and the urine small in volume and concentrated; without ADH, AQP2 is withdrawn from the luminal membrane, the duct is almost impermeable to water and a large volume of dilute urine is passed.

rows: High: AQP2 inserted into the luminal membrane
Low: AQP2 withdrawn from the luminal membrane
Water leaves the duct, down the gradient into the hypertonic medulla

blocks.title: Two kinds of diabetes insipidus
blocks.text: Diabetes insipidus is the passage of large volumes of dilute urine. In central diabetes insipidus ADH secretion is deficient; in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus ADH is present but the collecting duct does not respond (for example because of a V2 receptor or AQP2 defect, or lithium therapy). Do not confuse it with diabetes mellitus, where the diuresis is osmotic because of glucose in the urine.

points: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65 per cent of filtered Na+ and water isosmotically and all glucose and amino acids (below the transport maximum); the thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 25 per cent of Na+ via NKCC2 without water; the distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune Na+, K+, H+ and water.

The countercurrent multiplier uses active NaCl transport out of the water-impermeable thick ascending limb (the single effect) to build a medullary osmotic gradient up to about 1200 mOsm/kg; the vasa recta preserve it by countercurrent exchange, and urea recycling contributes.

ADH binds V2 receptors on principal cells and, through cAMP, inserts aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane, making the collecting duct permeable to water so that water follows the gradient into the medulla.
Without ADH the collecting duct is impermeable and dilute urine is produced; minimum urine volume equals solute load divided by maximum urine osmolality.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes reabsorption in the proximal tubule?

options.text: About two thirds of filtered sodium and water, and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids, are reabsorbed
Only the final 5 per cent of filtered sodium is reabsorbed
Water is reabsorbed but the fluid becomes markedly hypo-osmotic
Sodium is reabsorbed without water, diluting the tubular fluid

questions.correctOptionText: About two thirds of filtered sodium and water, and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids, are reabsorbed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65 per cent of the filtrate isosmotically, plus all of the glucose and amino acids.
distractorRationale.b: This is closer to the distal convoluted tubule's contribution.
distractorRationale.c: The proximal tubule is highly water-permeable, so the fluid stays approximately isosmotic.
distractorRationale.d: This describes the thick ascending limb, not the proximal tubule.

questions.explanation: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65 per cent of the filtered sodium and water in an isosmotic fashion, together with nearly all glucose, amino acids and much of the bicarbonate. The rest of the nephron adjusts what remains.

questions.stem: A loop diuretic acts by blocking a transporter in the thick ascending limb. Which transporter is it, and what is the immediate effect on water handling in this segment? (Pharmacology teaching example only.)

options.text: The Na+/Cl- cotransporter, which reduces reabsorption of water in this segment
The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter, which reduces solute reabsorption in a segment that is normally water-impermeable
The epithelial sodium channel, which makes the segment water-permeable
The sodium-glucose cotransporter, which reduces glucose reabsorption

questions.correctOptionText: The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter, which reduces solute reabsorption in a segment that is normally water-impermeable

distractorRationale.a: The Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC) is in the distal convoluted tubule and is the thiazide target.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb moves NaCl out without water; blocking it also weakens the medullary gradient.
distractorRationale.c: ENaC is in the collecting duct and the thick ascending limb is not water-permeable.
distractorRationale.d: SGLT2 is in the proximal tubule.

questions.explanation: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered sodium using the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter NKCC2 while remaining water-impermeable. Blocking it reduces NaCl reabsorption and also the medullary osmotic gradient, so a large volume of poorly concentrated urine results.

questions.stem: A patient with central diabetes insipidus has a urine osmolality fixed at 100 mOsm/L (taken as mOsm/kg) because there is no ADH. He must excrete 800 mOsm of solute per day. Calculate his daily urine volume in L/day.
questions.explanation: Volume equals solute load divided by urine osmolality, 800 / 100 = 8 L/day. Without ADH the collecting duct stays water-impermeable, so the kidney cannot concentrate the urine and the large volume of dilute urine must be replaced by drinking.

questions.stem: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus has a plasma glucose of 25 mmol/L and passes large volumes of urine containing glucose. Which mechanism best explains the glycosuria?

options.text: The filtered glucose load exceeds the transport maximum of proximal tubular carriers, so some glucose is not reabsorbed
Glucose is normally secreted by the distal tubule and secretion is increased
The glomerular barrier becomes more permeable to glucose than normal
ADH has reduced the permeability of the collecting duct to glucose

questions.correctOptionText: The filtered glucose load exceeds the transport maximum of proximal tubular carriers, so some glucose is not reabsorbed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the carriers saturate once plasma glucose passes the renal threshold.
distractorRationale.b: Glucose is not normally secreted by the distal tubule.
distractorRationale.c: Glucose is freely filtered even in health; the problem is reabsorption, not filtration.
distractorRationale.d: ADH acts on water permeability, not on glucose handling.

questions.explanation: Glucose is freely filtered and normally fully reabsorbed by proximal sodium-glucose cotransporters, which have a finite transport maximum. At very high plasma levels the filtered load exceeds this, and the unreabsorbed glucose appears in the urine and holds water with it.

questions.stem: Which feature of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle produces the 'single effect' of the countercurrent multiplier?

options.text: Active transport of NaCl out of the tubule while the wall remains impermeable to water
High permeability to water, so that water leaves freely
Active secretion of urea into the tubule
Insertion of aquaporin-2 under the action of ADH

questions.correctOptionText: Active transport of NaCl out of the tubule while the wall remains impermeable to water

distractorRationale.a: Correct: NaCl leaves without water, making the interstitium hypertonic and the tubular fluid dilute.
distractorRationale.b: The thick ascending limb is water-impermeable; water leaves the descending limb.
distractorRationale.c: Urea is not actively secreted into the thick ascending limb to produce the single effect.
distractorRationale.d: AQP2 insertion occurs in the collecting duct, not the thick ascending limb.

questions.explanation: The single effect is the difference in osmolality created across the wall of the thick ascending limb by active NaCl transport without water movement. This raises interstitial osmolality and is multiplied along the loop by the countercurrent flows.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the vasa recta in producing concentrated urine?

options.text: They actively pump NaCl into the medulla
They act as countercurrent exchangers, supplying the medulla with blood without washing away the osmotic gradient
They secrete ADH into the medullary interstitium
They are the site of aquaporin-2 insertion

questions.correctOptionText: They act as countercurrent exchangers, supplying the medulla with blood without washing away the osmotic gradient

distractorRationale.a: Active NaCl transport occurs in the thick ascending limb, not the vasa recta.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: blood gains solute going down and loses it coming up, so the gradient is preserved.
distractorRationale.c: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
distractorRationale.d: AQP2 is in collecting duct principal cells.

questions.explanation: The vasa recta are hairpin capillaries running alongside the loops of Henle. Their passive countercurrent exchange lets blood supply and drain the medulla while leaving the osmotic gradient built by the loops largely intact.

questions.stem: An older man excretes 750 mOsm of solute per day and his maximum urine concentrating ability is 1000 mOsm/L. Calculate the minimum daily urine volume (obligatory water loss) in L/day.
questions.explanation: Minimum volume equals solute load divided by the maximum urine osmolality, 750 / 1000 = 0.75 L/day. A kidney that cannot concentrate as well must lose more water to excrete the same solute, so it depends on the countercurrent system being intact.

questions.stem: How does antidiuretic hormone increase the water permeability of the collecting duct?

options.text: It binds V2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP and causing insertion of aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane of principal cells
It increases glomerular filtration rate
It increases NaCl transport in the thick ascending limb by blocking NKCC2
It opens the tight junctions between tubular cells

questions.correctOptionText: It binds V2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP and causing insertion of aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane of principal cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: V2 receptor signalling leads to AQP2 insertion in the luminal membrane.
distractorRationale.b: ADH does not act principally by raising GFR.
distractorRationale.c: ADH does not block NKCC2; that is the action of loop diuretics.
distractorRationale.d: ADH acts through water channels, not by opening tight junctions.

questions.explanation: ADH binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane, increasing cAMP and protein kinase A activity, which drives AQP2-containing vesicles to fuse with the luminal membrane. Water can then follow the osmotic gradient out of the lumen into the hypertonic medulla.

questions.stem: Describe how antidiuretic hormone alters the water permeability of the collecting duct, and contrast the urine produced in its presence with that produced in its absence.
markingGuide: ADH is released from the posterior pituitary in response to raised plasma osmolality or reduced blood volume
It binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of principal cells
Cyclic AMP rises and protein kinase A promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane
Water leaves the lumen via AQP2 and exits through AQP3 and AQP4 in the basolateral membrane, down the osmotic gradient into the hypertonic medulla
With ADH: small volume of concentrated urine, up to about 1200 mOsm/kg
Without ADH: AQP2 withdrawn, duct water-impermeable, large volume of dilute urine (about 50 mOsm/kg)
questions.explanation: ADH makes the collecting duct water-permeable by inserting aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane, so water follows the medullary osmotic gradient and urine is concentrated. Without ADH, the channels are withdrawn and dilute urine is passed in large volume.

questions.stem: Explain how the countercurrent multiplier in the loop of Henle generates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, and why this gradient allows the kidney to produce urine more concentrated than plasma only when ADH is present.
markingGuide: Thick ascending limb actively transports NaCl (via NKCC2) out of the tubule while impermeable to water: the single effect
This makes the interstitium hypertonic and dilutes the fluid in the limb
The descending limb is water-permeable, so water leaves and fluid becomes concentrated towards the tip
Opposed flow in the two limbs multiplies the small effect at each level into a gradient up to about 1200 mOsm/kg
Urea recycling and the vasa recta (countercurrent exchange) help to build and maintain the gradient
Fluid reaching the collecting duct is dilute, and concentrated urine requires water to leave the duct into the hypertonic medulla, which needs ADH-induced aquaporin-2 channels
Without ADH the duct stays impermeable so the urine remains dilute despite the gradient
questions.explanation: The thick ascending limb transports NaCl without water, and the opposed flows in the loop multiply this single effect into a steep medullary gradient, preserved by the vasa recta. The gradient is only a potential for concentration: water leaves the collecting duct to equilibrate with it only when ADH has inserted aquaporin-2 channels.
